segments.t: Mathias has brought Miranda back to speak with Cecile about the film. The role may be available again, but the offer comes with a demand about her appearance. Listen to the French first, following Cecile's changing reaction.
Quentin a réfléchi. Il te veut vraiment.
Merci, c'est super!
Mais il veut une femme plus jeune.
Si tu veux le rôle, tu dois changer.
Je ne comprends pas.
Tu as de la chance. Il faut juste faire les joues.
Une opération? Tu es sérieuse?
C'est du lipofilling.
C'est totalement différent.
Désolée, je ne touche pas à mon visage.
Attends, Cécile. Écoutons Miranda.
C'est tellement simple.
Et voilà, c'est terminé. Tête de bébé!
Non, c'est facile de dire terminé.
Elles commencent avec le Botox, puis elles ne s'arrêtent plus.
Tu veux jouer l'immortelle?
Oui, bien sûr, mais…
Je ne sais plus.
Let's go back through it. Miranda begins with promising news, but Cecile still has questions.
Quentin a réfléchi.
'Quentin has thought it over.' The past action uses 'have' and a short past form ending in a clear vowel sound. The thought is complete before this meeting begins.
Il te veut vraiment.
'He really wants you.' Miranda places the short object meaning 'you' before 'wants'. The final word strengthens her reassurance.
Merci, c'est super!
'Thanks, that's great!' The last word sounds just like its English cousin, and the French use it all the time for anything they like. But then comes the catch.
Mais il veut une femme plus jeune.
'But he wants a younger woman.' The comparison literally says 'more young'. The small word for 'more' goes before the description, as Miranda explains the problem.
Si tu veux le rôle, tu dois changer.
'If you want the part, you have to change.' The second half uses the verb 'must'. Cécile doesn't see what he means.
Je ne comprends pas.
'I don't understand.' Notice the two little negative words around the verb. Keep that in mind; there's a variation at the end of the scene.
Tu as de la chance.
'You're lucky.' Literally 'you have some luck'. French often uses 'to have' where English uses 'to be'.
Il faut juste faire les joues.
'You just need to have your cheeks done.' The first two words mean 'it is necessary', a very handy way to say what has to happen, without saying who. Cécile can't believe it.
Une opération? Tu es sérieuse?
'An operation? Are you serious?' Cecile uses the feminine form of 'serious' because she is questioning Miranda. The rising voice makes it a question without a special question expression.
C'est du lipofilling.
'It's lipofilling.' The small word before the treatment name introduces an unspecified amount. Miranda gives it a technical name to make the proposal sound less alarming.
C'est totalement différent.
'It's totally different.' The long word before 'different' means 'completely'. It strengthens the producer's claim rather than naming a different procedure.
Désolée, je ne touche pas à mon visage.
'Sorry, I'm not touching my face.' The word for 'sorry' has a feminine ending, because Cécile is a woman.
Attends, Cécile. Écoutons Miranda.
'Wait, Cécile. Let's listen to Miranda.' This second command ends in the sound for 'let's', which means 'we' are doing it together. Miranda makes it sound like nothing.
C'est tellement simple.
'It's so simple.' The middle word means 'so' or 'really', and it makes anything stronger.
Et voilà, c'est terminé. Tête de bébé!
'And there you go, it's done. Baby face!' The first short expression presents a finished result, like 'there you are'. Miranda makes the change sound quick and easy.
Non, c'est facile de dire terminé.
'No, it's easy to say done.' She throws Miranda's own word back at her. Then she says what she's seen around her.
Elles commencent avec le Botox, puis elles ne s'arrêtent plus.
'They start with Botox, then they don't stop anymore.' The second negative word means 'anymore', replacing ordinary 'not'. Here 'they' refers to other women having cosmetic treatments.
Tu veux jouer l'immortelle?
'Do you want to play the immortal woman?' The character's title is feminine, so the article and its ending refer to a woman. The part is the one Cecile still hopes to play.
Oui, bien sûr, mais…
'Yes, of course, but…' The final small word promises a qualification. Cecile leaves it unfinished because she is still unsure.
Je ne sais plus.

'I don't know anymore.' Compare it with 'I don't know', which would end with the usual negative word. Here, the word for 'anymore' takes its place. One small swap, and you go from not knowing to no longer knowing. Here's the scene again from start to finish. Now let's listen to the entire dialogue once more.
Quentin a réfléchi. Il te veut vraiment.
Merci, c'est super!
Mais il veut une femme plus jeune.
Si tu veux le rôle, tu dois changer.
Je ne comprends pas.
Tu as de la chance. Il faut juste faire les joues.
Une opération? Tu es sérieuse?
C'est du lipofilling.
C'est totalement différent.
Désolée, je ne touche pas à mon visage.
Attends, Cécile. Écoutons Miranda.
C'est tellement simple.
Et voilà, c'est terminé. Tête de bébé!
Non, c'est facile de dire terminé.
Elles commencent avec le Botox, puis elles ne s'arrêtent plus.
Tu veux jouer l'immortelle?
Oui, bien sûr, mais…
Je ne sais plus.
That's a hard choice for Cécile, and a good one for you to remember: 'not' and 'not anymore' are built the same way, only the second little word changes. See you next time!
À bientôt!
